one_liner: Opt-in wasm simd128 versions of strlen, memchr, strchr, strrchr, memcmp, strspn and strcspn in wasi-libc, replacing musl's scalar loops.
what_it_does: wasi-libc is the standard C library for WASI targets (the libc in wasi-sdk's sysroot). Building it with the CMake option -DSIMD=ON defines __wasilibc_simd_string and compiles SIMD bodies for strlen, memchr, __strchrnul (and so strchr), __memrchr (and so strrchr), memcmp, strspn and strcspn. The API is the unchanged <string.h>, so it is a drop-in at the sysroot level: relink against a SIMD-built libc.a and existing code picks it up.
how_it_is_fast: Each routine scans 16 bytes per step with v128 compares (i8x16.eq) and a cheap any_true/all_true test, only computing i8x16.bitmask plus ctz/clz once a hit is found, because bitmask lowers poorly on AArch64. strlen, memchr, strchrnul, strspn and strcspn load aligned 16-byte blocks (reading slightly before and after the object, safe because wasm memory is bounds-checked at 64 KiB page granularity) through inline assembly so the compiler cannot treat the over-read as UB; memcmp and memrchr use unaligned v128 loads strictly inside [0, n). strspn/strcspn use the Langdale/Mula nibble-bitmap byte-set lookup (the same idea as Hyperscan's truffle) with two i8x16.swizzle table lookups per block.
when_to_use: You build your own wasi-libc sysroot (wasi-sdk does not pass -DSIMD=ON) and your runtime supports simd128 (and relaxed-simd for strspn/strcspn).
String-heavy C code compiled to wasm, such as SQLite, parsers or text tools, where strlen/memchr/strchr scans over strings of tens of bytes or more dominate.
memcmp-heavy code on buffers of 16 bytes or more, and strrchr or memrchr scans, where the musl fallback is a byte-at-a-time loop and the SIMD gain is largest.
Hosts on AArch64 or x86-64 with a JIT/AOT runtime (wasmtime, wazero, V8) that lowers v128 ops to NEON or SSE.
when_not_to_use: Your toolchain is Clang 19 or 20: strlen, memchr, strchr, strspn and strcspn silently fall back to scalar (llvm/llvm-project#146574 ICE guard); only memcmp and memrchr/strrchr get SIMD.
You need strcmp, strncmp, strstr, memmem or strcasecmp speedups: those stay scalar musl code in wasi-libc (the larger numbers in issue #580 came from ncruces's separate go-sqlite3 libc).
Interpreted or non-SIMD wasm runtimes, or runtimes without relaxed-simd: a module containing i8x16.relaxed_swizzle (strspn_simd.c) will fail validation.
Very short strings or calls dominated by host/call overhead; the only small-string data point is about 2x for 10-byte strlen under wasmtime, and no per-size table exists.
You want a stock prebuilt sysroot: the SIMD build is opt-in and off by default, so using it means maintaining a custom wasi-libc build.

integration.dependencies: none beyond wasi-libc's own build (clang with the wasm32 target, compiler-rt builtins)
integration.min_toolchain: Clang 10+ for wasi-libc; SIMD string paths need Clang 21+ (Clang 19/20 compile the scalar fallback for the inline-asm routines); build flags -msimd128 -mrelaxed-simd -mbulk-memory
integration.platforms: wasm32 (wasip1, wasip2, wasip1-threads, ...) on runtimes with simd128; relaxed-simd needed for the SIMD strspn/strcspn
integration.thread_safety: Pure functions with no shared state; thread-safe like the scalar versions

gotchas: Test-coverage gap: wasi-libc's only SIMD CI job ('Test wasm32-wasi-simd', -DSIMD=ON) uses clang_version 20, which compiles out the inline-asm SIMD paths, so upstream CI exercises only the SIMD memcmp and memrchr; strlen, memchr, strchrnul, strspn and strcspn SIMD code is validated only by the contributor's Go tests and fuzzing and by abrown's out-of-tree fuzzing.

Latent C undefined behaviour in strspn_simd.c's __wasm_v128_setbit: bitmap->hi[lo_nibble] |= (uint8_t)(1u << (hi_nibble - 8)) shifts by a negative count for every byte below 0x80. It works today only because wasm's i32.shl masks the count to 5 bits, giving 1<<24..31 which truncates to 0; the shift line came up in PR #597 review but UB was not discussed.

The 'over musl's SWAR' framing is only true for strlen, memchr and strchrnul: the scalar memcmp, memrchr, strcmp and strncmp in wasi-libc are byte-at-a-time loops and strspn/strcspn use a bitset loop, which is why memcmp (10.0x) and strrchr (9.9x) show the largest gains.

memcmp and memrchr SIMD assume the whole n-byte range is readable: abrown's fuzzing found a 16-byte memcmp near the end of memory that traps in the SIMD version while the scalar version returns early (invalid input either way; documented in the source comment).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it whenever the target is wasm and the libc is wasi-libc: Arm Optimized Routines, AOCL-LibMem and the other native siblings cannot be used inside a wasm module, and the WebAssembly memory.copy entry only covers memcpy/memmove/memset, not search and compare routines. For native code use Arm Optimized Routines or the host glibc instead.
verified_claims_summary: The only per-function table (memchr 4.3x, memcmp 10.0x, strlen 4.9x, strchr 4.2x, strrchr 9.9x, strspn 9.1x, strcspn 9.7x over the musl scalar code) is a rough comment by the contributor in issue #580, measured with Go under wazero on GitHub Actions x86-64 and AArch64 runners against his go-sqlite3 libc, with no CPU model, string sizes, compiler or flags; PR #586 adds about 3x strlen and 2x memchr on mixed lengths (7x and 5x on large inputs) and about 2x for 10-byte strlen under wasmtime on amd64. The SIMD-versus-scalar comparison is wasm-to-wasm within the same libc, not against native glibc.
status_note: Actively maintained WebAssembly-organisation project (commits through 2026-10-01) under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, Apache-2.0 and MIT; the SIMD routines landed between June and December 2025 and remain opt-in, with maintainers asking for real-world users before considering enabling them by default.
